cards.title: Build a Bill of Materials Before Anything Else
cards.summary: A bill of materials breaks unit cost into every component and sub-vendor so COGS becomes a controllable, negotiable line instead of a mystery number.
cards.use_when: Setting up or renegotiating product sourcing for any physical-goods store, and before you start sourcing a new SKU or assume your landed cost is fixed.
steps: List every component of the finished unit (e.g. a gold solitaire ring = diamond, gold, labor, factory overhead, factory margin).
For each component, capture: component cost, sub-supplier/source, lead time, country of origin, and payment terms.
Get the sub-vendor layer too — your factory may not make its own inputs (lab-grown diamonds, gold, zippers, chipsets).

Split out labor and factory overhead as separate lines; these are the hardest to ask about but the ones that reveal where the money is. Verify sourcing claims (e.g. test that 'organic cotton' is actually organic).
Track component prices that move intraday or monthly (gold, diamonds, chipsets) so a supplier's markup stays visible and you can reprice when markets move.
Review the BOM with your supplier at least yearly and request price-break thresholds per line item.
Use the BOM as the first audit when acquiring or taking over a store: ~99 of 100 founders in the source's M&A experience did not have one.
caveats: The source says a BOM is worth building once you spend roughly $1M/year on COGS (~$100k/month to supplier), and some businesses benefit as low as ~$2.5M annual revenue; it is a judgment call below that.

cards.title: Use BOM to Rethink Product Specs, Not Just Costs
cards.summary: Once you see every component's cost, you can engineer margin by changing materials, karat purity, or SKU tiers rather than only squeezing the supplier.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and product-development decisions — deciding what materials, specs, and SKU variants to sell and at what price.
steps: After building the BOM, ask structural questions per SKU: can this be made in a cheaper input (e.g. 10K vs 14K gold)? Can a premium tier be offered that lets you raise price more than cost?
Test whether a higher-end variant can be priced $200 above the base version while adding only ~$100 of real cost, creating more absolute dollars of margin.
Check whether you actually need every spec — if a component is a small share of COGS, price is your lever; if it's a large share, material substitution is your lever.
Feed these findings back into product selection so you choose SKUs whose component structure you can actually control.
Keep monitoring the component markets: a price move can swing a SKU's economics and force a repricing decision.
caveats: The source's example: Linear raised prices ~six times in 18 months as gold rose and still grew, because luxury-brand competitors left a gap — do not assume your category has that pricing power.

cards.title: Enter Supplier Negotiations From a Position of Redundancy
cards.summary: Before asking a supplier to cut cost, do your homework so you already know the benchmark cost and have alternate suppliers mapped — leverage comes from preparation.
cards.use_when: Preparing for a cost-down negotiation with a factory or new supplier, or onboarding a supplier for a new product line.
steps: Before negotiating, buy and reverse-engineer competitor samples and map alternative suppliers for every key component.
Talk to heads of procurement at larger incumbent brands in your category to learn the industry-standard factory margin band (e.g. the source cites jewelry factories at ~5–9% EBITDA).
Come in with the BOM already drafted from other suppliers so the conversation starts from knowledge, not hope.
Ask each supplier to build their own BOM to your template rather than sending your current supplier's BOM — you want their independently sourced component costs.
Always maintain at least one viable alternate factory so you can act if the incumbent won't move.
caveats: The source's rule: if the factory won't budge, find another factory — but this only works if you actually built the redundancy first. If you entered the relationship giving the factory too much power, leverage is hard to recover.

cards.title: Frame Cost-Downs as a Growth Partnership, Not a Squeeze
cards.summary: Present cost reduction to suppliers as fueling volume growth for both sides — share your P&L vision and translate it into units and dollars they care about.
cards.use_when: Making the first cost-down request to an existing factory, or resetting terms after acquiring a store or scaling a product line.
steps: Signal new ownership or new ambition explicitly ('I bought this because I plan to 5x it'), then explain you want both parties to win.
Share an abstracted P&L (e.g. 20% COGS, 40% marketing, 10% profit) and show where the savings go — funnel them into marketing to drive more volume, not into your pocket.
Translate the growth vision into units, since factories care about units, not your ad spend: 'we buy 1M units now, we want 10M by 2030.'
Walk them through the price-break thresholds you need per component and ask when each line item drops.
Offer to split financing or cost burden to show partnership (the source paid 80% of financing cost, factory 20% in one case).
Test whether their margin is abnormal for your industry before pushing hard — opening your books makes the conversation collaborative rather than confrontational.
caveats: This works only if you have a credible growth story and (ideally) benchmarks for normal margins in the category; a supplier with thin margins has nothing to give.

cards.title: Ask for Volume Price Breaks on Every BOM Line
cards.summary: Negotiate component-level price breaks tied to unit volumes, understanding that factory economics rest on machine and labor utilization.
cards.use_when: Setting up volume tiers with a factory, planning a purchase order schedule, or forecasting COGS at higher volumes.
steps: For each BOM line (cotton, labor, zippers, polishing/QC, etc.), ask: at what volume does this price drop?
Frame it around the supplier's utilization — how much of their dedicated line is used, where is idle machine or fixed-labor capacity you can fill?
Reconcile invoices with the supplier line-by-line (the source has production leads sit with suppliers to do this), so credits for hitting thresholds are actually applied.
Track price breaks on sub-components too, since suppliers pass through their own sub-vendor economies of scale (e.g. a big zipper maker gives the factory a discount that should flow to you).

Consider internalizing procurement of key components (buying gold/diamonds/chips directly and supplying your assembler) to capture the sub-vendor margin, but only once you can manage the inventory price risk.
caveats: The source frames these as credits applied after you hit overage volumes, not blanket discounts — build the mechanism into the agreement. Internalizing components also exposes you to commodity price swings.

cards.title: Use Payment Terms to Widen Your Float, Not to Chase Sales
cards.summary: Your real float is payment terms minus production lead time, so extending net terms buys you error tolerance and free cash flow.
cards.use_when: Deciding what payment terms to request from suppliers and how much working capital to hold before scaling ad spend or order volume.
steps: Calculate float: e.g. 90-day terms minus 30-day production+shipping = 60 days of float; if lead time is 45–90 days and you're on net 30, you're actually negative.
Push for longer net terms as you mature — the source went from net 7 to net 90, citing net 180 as an extreme others use.
Recognize the most valuable outcome is margin of error: marketing is a daily variable cost you can switch off, a purchase order is not.
Factor in inventory mistakes (e.g. wrong size mix on rings) that eat your float in the real world.
Target consignment if you can get it: the factory owns goods until you sell, converting a made-to-order business to near-dropship cash dynamics.
caveats: Consignment is easiest with categories where the supplier can reclaim/resell inventory (the source notes gold's melt value and Hong Kong fulfillment made it feasible for one business); it isn't universally available.

cards.title: Understand Supplier Financing to Unlock Better Terms
cards.summary: Factories use credit insurance and invoice factoring, so your P&L, not just the PO, determines the terms you can get — clean books matter.
cards.use_when: Negotiating extended terms or consignment, and when a supplier says they can't afford to float you.
steps: Know the supplier's mechanics: they buy credit insurance against customer defaults, then their bank factors the invoice (e.g. ~99 cents on the dollar), paying financing cost as an annual rate (the source cites ~6% in China).
This means the supplier can often pass longer terms onto you at a low cost, so ask them to show the financing line in their BOM.
Support the credit audit: credit insurers grade you A/B/C using management accounts and payment history, and a past dispute can land you a low grade that blocks terms.
Keep books clean and pay on time to maintain a good grade — an unresolved supplier dispute from years prior cost the source a C rating.
Add financing cost as an explicit BOM line so the burden-sharing conversation is concrete (e.g. '$6/unit now, $5 if we double volume').
caveats: Rating is done by the insurer, not the factory, and low grades block financing; it can take time and effort to repair. Works best where the supplier is in a credit-insured export ecosystem (e.g. China).

cards.title: Turn Your Supplier Into Your Bank
cards.summary: The goal across BOM, price breaks and terms is a supplier relationship where they finance your inventory and dividends.
cards.use_when: Designing your overall sourcing/finance strategy and deciding what to prioritize as you scale purchasing.
steps: Stack the levers in order: BOM for cost visibility, then component price breaks, then long payment terms, then consignment.

Use the supplier's financing to fund growth instead of taking high-cost third-party ecommerce loans — the source warns that lenders whose cost rises with your growth can turn an advertised ~10% into 30–40% effective cost.
Compare financing cost against revenue, not COGS: 6% of COGS may be a rounding error on the P&L.
Keep the supplier relationship collaborative and share your vision so they become an eager partner rather than a lender of last resort.
Treat favorable terms as your primary growth capital and reinvest savings into marketing.
caveats: This is Roman Khan's stated approach; results are his own and reflect a specific business mix and scale, not a guarantee. Long terms and consignment still require a supplier willing to extend them.

cards.title: Build Component-Redundancy and Market-Monitoring Discipline
cards.summary: Actively re-source commodity components on an ongoing basis rather than one-time — keep multiple vendors and spot-check market prices.
cards.use_when: Managing replenishment and ongoing COGS after initial sourcing is set up.
steps: For commodities with public pricing (e.g. gold, lab-grown diamonds), pull current market prices monthly; diamonds in particular need quotes from 6–7 sub-vendors per month.
Attend the main industry trade fairs (the source notes chipset fairs that happen twice a year) to meet alternative and better suppliers, not just keep your current one.
Expect the supplier to carry an inventory-risk markup on top of component cost; that markup is your negotiation target.
Track component price moves that can force a repricing or spec change, and decide proactively: raise price (and test whether volume holds) or substitute materials.
Consider a hedging/diversification posture: the source notes buying components directly can also let you profit on a commodity rally, though this adds risk.
caveats: Component concentration risk is real — the source notes one supplier made up ~70% of COGS. Fully internalizing procurement exposes you directly to commodity volatility and inventory risk.

cards.title: Pause Growth When Input and Tariff Shocks Hit
cards.summary: When duties, tariffs or commodity moves make the unit economics unsafe, it is acceptable to deliberately slow growth and hold flat while you rework sourcing.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment and sourcing planning when tariffs, duties, or input costs spike and your margins are compressed.
steps: Map your product's exposure: where is it produced (country of origin) and what duties/tariffs apply, from your BOM's country-of-origin column.

If exposure is unmanageable, decide explicitly to hold revenue flat rather than push volume at broken economics (the source paused growth for about a year on an India-produced business during high tariffs).
Use the pause to renegotiate with the supplier — if their margins were inflated, ask for a concession while conditions are bad.
As duties recede, be ready to resume growth and expect to give some margin back to the supplier ('pay a little more for COGS').
caveats: This is a scale- and category-specific move from the source; not every business can afford a flat year. The trade relationship with the supplier is central — transparent BOM data made the concession conversation possible.

cards.title: Close Books Monthly and Dividend From Free Cash, Not EBITDA
cards.summary: Track actual cash generation monthly and fund only needed working capital before taking distributions — EBITDA is not cash.
cards.use_when: Setting a monthly schedule for taking money out of the store and deciding how much cash to retain to fund growth.
steps: Close the books by the 15th of each month for the prior month: revenue, COGS (cash and accrual), opex, profit.
Separate EBITDA from free cash flow — the source stresses the gap between profit and cash actually in the bank.
Estimate the working capital the coming months require for planned growth before withdrawing anything (e.g. if growing 80%, size the reserve accordingly).
Only dividend what is genuinely free after that reserve; the source projects taking ~65–75% of free cash flow out as distributions.
Automate/pre-derive the process so monthly distributions become routine, turning profit into actual cash in your account.
caveats: The source's distribution range is his own projection, not a universal benchmark. Without management accounts (the source says ~70% of the M&A founders he meets lack them), this is not possible — the cadence has to be built first.

cards.title: Audit Margin Reality: COGS Is Your Biggest Lever
cards.summary: Opex and marketing are relatively predictable; COGS is the biggest controllable swing factor, which is why sourcing discipline beats growth-at-all-costs.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend optimization effort — sourcing vs marketing vs overhead — and reviewing whether your business is genuinely profitable in cash terms.
steps: Break the P&L into revenue, COGS, marketing, overhead; note that overhead and mature marketing are fairly predictable, while COGS is the largest moving variable.
Compare component-price moves (e.g. COGS jumping from ~15% to ~30% of revenue if gold doubles) against your ability to reprice or substitute.
Focus cost-down effort on COGS sourcing rather than assuming it's fixed; you can always find new vendors, whereas ad costs follow platform rules.
Measure true margin bands and recognize that sub-10% EBITDA becomes fragile under a single rental, platform, or freight shock.
Decide whether your category is genuinely profitable enough to keep scaling or whether you need to change the product/sourcing structure first.
caveats: The source's benchmark observations (many stores sub-10% EBITDA, some 20–25%) come from his own M&A pipeline and may not represent your category. He is openly 'dividend first,' which prioritizes cash extraction over growth velocity — a value judgment, not a universal rule.
